text:
[NCBK.2.9] **`DS_EV_ENGINE_ERROR` is the last gasp: the integrator **must
not** resume service on that engine.** After it, the integrator **must not**
make any `ds_engine_*` call on that engine but the ones this clause names as
valid below — not a pump, not an assert or retract, not a load or a
registration, not a configuration or callback setter, not `ds_engine_clone`,
which would carry the halted state into an engine with no halt, and not a read
of working memory, a schema or the introspection surface. The tier has halted
([LERR.1.4.7]).

**The engine must refuse each such call with `DS_ERR_ENGINE_HALTED`, and must
not act on it.** The halt is a latch: the engine sets it when it raises the
`EngineError` and never clears it. The
refusal is the same code whatever caused the halt; the cause is the
`EngineError`'s payload ([NCBK.2.10]). Refusing consults the latch and nothing
else, so it is a guarantee an engine whose state is untrustworthy can still
honour.

**A failed load sets the latch too** ([RDSC.9.8]). A `ds_engine_load_dsc` that
fails once it has begun reading the artefact returns the error that stopped
it, delivers no event, and leaves the latch set: every later call is refused
as above, but the four this clause names. A load refused with `DS_ERR_INVAL`
or `DS_ERR_STATE`, or on an engine already halted, sets nothing.

**The call that raises the `EngineError` stops at it** ([LERR.1.4.7]). It
fires, propagates and records nothing after the `EngineError`, not even the
close of the activation that raised it (its end annotation and its
`scope activation` retractions). So the `EngineError` is the last stream
event the integrator receives from that engine.

**The call that raises the `EngineError` reports the halt too.** A public call during which the engine raises an
`EngineError` — a pump whose firing faults, an assert or retract whose
propagation does — **must** return `DS_ERR_ENGINE_HALTED`, ahead of any other
status the call would have returned ([NCBK.1.5]). The one exception is a halt
whose clause gives it a code of its own, which that call returns instead, and
the only such clause is deferred ([RTCT.7.3], [NERR.18]). So a host that reads only statuses
learns of the halt from the call that caused it, and is never told `DS_OK` by
it. A replay is outside this sentence: a halt it re-derives is the recording's
content, and its status says whether it reproduced the run ([RFCS.6.7]).

**A read of engine state is refused too.** After
the halt the engine's state is undefined ([LERR.1.4.7]), so a working-memory,
schema or introspection read has no answer an integrator could rely on. The
engine **must** refuse it with `DS_ERR_ENGINE_HALTED`, by consulting the latch,
as it refuses a mutation. A fact lookup by id ([NFCT.6.4]) is such a read.

**So is a read through a fact or schema handle, whenever the handle was taken.**
Its one window is the call that raises the
`EngineError`: the records that call delivers ahead of the `EngineError`
([RFCS.6.7]) carry handles the integrator reads to make sense of them. The
engine **must** answer a handle read until it has delivered the `EngineError`
or the call that raised it has returned, and **must** refuse it with
`DS_ERR_ENGINE_HALTED` from then on.

**Four calls remain valid, because none of them reads that state.** The engine
**must** answer each after the halt:

- `ds_engine_halted`, which reads the latch and the fault that set it
  ([NCBK.2.11]);
- `ds_engine_get_platform_signature` and `ds_engine_get_session_header`, which
  report what was fixed at load: the provenance a recording of the halted run
  is filed under ([NDET.2.1]);
- `ds_engine_free` (below).

`[LERR.1.4.7]` says the **engine** halts the tier, which is a statement about
what the engine does; this clause says what the integrator may no longer
do. An integrator reading only that clause would take "halted" to mean "stops
firing rules" and go on pumping, which is the reading the word invites.

**The callback may still complete its own work.** The obligation is on calls
**into** the engine, not on the callback body: an integrator may log the event,
flush their own sink, signal a supervisor, and return. What they may not do is
re-enter, and a read is re-entry too: inside the callback every call on that
engine returns `DS_ERR_STATE` ([RARC.13.16]). The calls above that remain valid
are valid once the callback has returned.

**Teardown is not a call into a running engine.** `ds_engine_free` remains valid
and remains the integrator's responsibility — otherwise a halted tier would leak
everything it holds. It is valid once the callback has returned, as the others
are: from inside a callback on that engine it returns `DS_ERR_STATE` and frees
nothing, since freeing there would free the stack the callback returns into
([RARC.13.16]). The engine **must** release everything it holds whatever
state the halt left it in.
